### Module 07: Spatial Epidemiology

# Spatial Autocorrelation & Moran's I

***
**Learning objectives**
- Understand spatial autocorrelation: Tobler's First Law of Geography
- Build spatial weights matrices (queen contiguity, rook, distance-based, k-NN)
- Compute Global Moran's I and its significance via analytic tests
- Calculate Local Moran's I (LISA) to identify spatial clusters
- Produce cluster maps: High-High, Low-Low, High-Low, Low-High quadrants
- Interpret Moran scatterplots for health outcomes
- Compare LISA with Getis-Ord G* hot-spot analysis

**Data:** `Data/usa_data.csv` — CDC adult diabetes prevalence and County Health Rankings covariates for 3,108 US counties (CONUS + DC)  
**Geometries:** `Data/US_COUNTY.shp` — county polygons in NAD83 Albers (EPSG:5070)  
**Estimated time:** 3 hours | **Level:** Advanced  
**Libraries:** `sf`, `spdep`, `ggplot2`, `dplyr`, `patchwork`

## 1. Setup & US County Health Dataset

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(spdep)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(42)
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "mod07")
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
)

theme_map <- function() {
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, hjust = 0.5),
      legend.position = "right"
    )
}

# County Health Rankings + CDC diabetes prevalence (CONUS + DC)
raw <- read_csv("Data/usa_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Centroids stored as NAD83 Albers metres (EPSG:5070) — convert to WGS84 lon/lat
pts <- st_as_sf(raw, coords = c("centroid_x_m", "centroid_y_m"), crs = 5070, remove = FALSE)
pts_ll <- st_transform(pts, 4326)
xy <- st_coordinates(pts_ll)

df <- tibble(
  county_id       = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(raw$fips)),
  fips            = as.integer(raw$fips),
  county          = raw$county,
  state_abbr      = raw$state_abbr,
  state_name      = raw$state_name,
  lon             = xy[, 1],
  lat             = xy[, 2],
  x_m             = raw$centroid_x_m,
  y_m             = raw$centroid_y_m,
  diabetes_prev   = raw$y_diabetes_prevalence_adults_with_diabetes,
  pct_65plus      = raw$chr_65_and_older_65_and_over,
  pct_exercise    = raw$chr_access_to_exercise_opportunities,
  pct_obesity     = raw$chr_adult_obesity,
  food_env_index  = raw$chr_food_environment_index,
  n_pcp           = raw$chr_primary_care_physicians,
  rural_pop       = raw$chr_rural,
  n_unemployed    = raw$chr_unemployment,
  n_uninsured     = raw$chr_uninsured
)

# Standardised prevalence ratio: county rate / national mean (SMR analogue)
df$smr <- df$diabetes_prev / mean(df$diabetes_prev, na.rm = TRUE)

N_COUNTIES <- nrow(df)
cat(sprintf(
  "County dataset: N=%d | Diabetes: %.1f%% (SD=%.1f)\n",
  N_COUNTIES, mean(df$diabetes_prev), sd(df$diabetes_prev)
))
cat(sprintf(
  "Obesity: %.1f%% | 65+: %.1f%% | Food env. index: %.1f\n",
  mean(df$pct_obesity), mean(df$pct_65plus), mean(df$food_env_index)
))
```

Join tabular health data with US county polygons. Shannon County, SD (FIPS 46113) was renamed Oglala Lakota County (46102); recode before the join so the geometries match current FIPS.

```{r}
county_shapes <- st_read("Data/US_COUNTY.shp", quiet = TRUE)
county_shapes$FIPS <- as.integer(county_shapes$FIPS)
# Shannon County SD (46113) was renamed Oglala Lakota (46102)
county_shapes$FIPS[county_shapes$FIPS == 46113] <- 46102

gdf <- county_shapes %>%
  inner_join(df, by = c("FIPS" = "fips"))
bb <- st_bbox(gdf)

cat(sprintf("sf object: %d counties | CRS: %s\n", nrow(gdf), st_crs(gdf)$input))
cat(sprintf(
  "Bounding box (Albers metres): xmin=%.0f ymin=%.0f xmax=%.0f ymax=%.0f\n",
  bb["xmin"], bb["ymin"], bb["xmax"], bb["ymax"]
))
```

## 2. Spatial Weights Matrix

A **spatial weights matrix W** encodes the neighbourhood structure:
- **Queen contiguity**: shares any boundary point or corner
- **Rook contiguity**: shares an edge only
- **Distance-based**: $w_{ij} = 1$ if distance $<$ threshold
- **k-NN**: each unit connected to its $k$ nearest neighbours
- **Inverse distance**: $w_{ij} = 1/d_{ij}$ (continuous)

Row-standardisation: $W^*$ where each row sums to 1 (so $W^*x$ = spatial lag of $x$).

With 3,108 counties we **never** materialise a dense $n \times n$ matrix. `spdep` stores neighbours as an `nb` list and row-standardised weights as a `listw` object. Isolated island counties (no contiguous neighbour) are retained with `zero.policy = TRUE`: their spatial lag is set to 0 rather than `NA`.

```{r}
# Queen contiguity from county polygons
nb_queen <- poly2nb(gdf, queen = TRUE)
lw_queen <- nb2listw(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# k-nearest neighbours (k = 6) from Albers centroids (metres)
coords <- cbind(gdf$x_m, gdf$y_m)
nb_knn <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 6))
lw_knn <- nb2listw(nb_knn, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# Distance band: twice the 90th percentile of nearest-neighbour distance
nn1  <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 1))
nn_d <- unlist(nbdists(nn1, coords))
thr  <- as.numeric(2 * quantile(nn_d, 0.90))
nb_dist <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, thr)
lw_dist <- nb2listw(nb_dist, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

n <- nrow(gdf)
n_iso <- sum(card(nb_queen) == 0)
cat(sprintf("Queen W: %dx%d | Mean neighbours: %.1f | Isolated islands: %d\n",
            n, n, mean(card(nb_queen)), n_iso))
cat(sprintf("KNN W  : %dx%d | Mean neighbours: %.1f\n",
            n, n, mean(card(nb_knn))))
cat(sprintf("Dist W : %dx%d | Mean neighbours: %.1f | threshold = %.0f m\n",
            n, n, mean(card(nb_dist)), thr))
if (n_iso > 0) {
  cat("Island counties have zero queen neighbours; lags use zero.policy = TRUE.\n")
}
```

Queen contiguity is the default for the rest of this notebook (and for NB-03). k-NN and distance-band weights are useful sensitivity checks: k-NN guarantees every county has neighbours (no islands), while a distance band can leave remote counties unconnected.

## 3. Global Moran's I

### What is Global Moran's I? (Math for Dummies)

Global Moran's I is a single number that tells you whether places on a map with high (or low) values are clustered together, or scattered randomly.

#### Math intuition (for dummies!):
- Imagine you have values for every county, like the adult diabetes prevalence.
- For each county, look at its value and the values of its neighbours (using a weights matrix $W$).
- Moran's I compares:
  - Are high values near other high values, and low near low? (clustering, Moran's I $> 0$)
  - Are high and low values mixed up? (random, Moran's I $\approx 0$)
  - Are high values near low, and vice versa? (checkerboard, Moran's I $< 0$)

**The "for dummies" math:**

1. First, for each county, subtract the average rate from its value. This gives you "how much above or below average is this county?" Call this $z$.
2. Do the same for all counties so you have a list of $z$'s.
3. Look up the neighbours for each county (using $W$), and see if a county's $z$ is similar to its neighbours' $z$'s.
4. Moran's I formula looks like:

$$
I = \frac{N}{\sum W} \times \frac{\sum_i z_i \left( \sum_j W_{ij} z_j \right)}{\sum_i z_i^2}
$$

- **$N$**: Number of counties
- **$W$**: The matrix showing who's neighbours with whom
- **$z$**: Values after subtracting the mean

- If "like is near like" a lot, $I$ is positive and big.
- If there's no pattern, $I$ is close to zero.
- If opposites are neighbours, $I$ is negative.

**In short:** Moran's I = "Do neighbours tend to be similar, or not?"

We use `spdep::moran.test()` (analytic randomisation moments) for the multi-variable table. A permutation histogram for diabetes uses `moran.mc()` with `nsim = 199` — 999 draws are more precise but slow on 3,108 counties; 199 is enough to see that the observed $I$ sits far in the tail.

```{r}
moran_one <- function(x, lw, label) {
  mt <- moran.test(x, lw, zero.policy = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided")
  tibble(
    variable = label,
    I        = unname(mt$estimate["Moran I statistic"]),
    E_I      = unname(mt$estimate["Expectation"]),
    z_score  = unname(mt$statistic),
    p_value  = mt$p.value
  )
}

moran_tab <- bind_rows(
  moran_one(gdf$diabetes_prev,  lw_queen, "Diabetes (%)"),
  moran_one(gdf$pct_obesity,    lw_queen, "Obesity (%)"),
  moran_one(gdf$pct_65plus,     lw_queen, "Population 65+ (%)"),
  moran_one(gdf$food_env_index, lw_queen, "Food env. index"),
  moran_one(gdf$n_pcp,          lw_queen, "PCP count"),
  moran_one(gdf$n_uninsured,    lw_queen, "Uninsured (count)"),
  moran_one(gdf$smr,            lw_queen, "SPR")
)
print(moran_tab, n = Inf)

res_diab <- moran.test(gdf$diabetes_prev, lw_queen,
                       zero.policy = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided")
mc_diab  <- moran.mc(gdf$diabetes_prev, lw_queen, nsim = 199,
                     zero.policy = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
I_diab   <- unname(res_diab$estimate["Moran I statistic"])
e_diab   <- unname(res_diab$estimate["Expectation"])
p_diab   <- res_diab$p.value
cat(sprintf(
  "\nDiabetes Moran's I = %.4f (E[I]=%.4f, z=%.2f, analytic p=%.4g; MC nsim=199 p=%.4g)\n",
  I_diab, e_diab, unname(res_diab$statistic), p_diab, mc_diab$p.value
))
```

The Global Moran's I statistic quantifies the overall spatial autocorrelation of the variable across the study area.

- A **positive** and significant Moran's I ($p < 0.05$) indicates that areas with high (or low) values cluster together — there is spatial clustering of similar values (either hot spots or cold spots).
- A **negative** Moran's I suggests spatial dispersion — neighbouring areas tend to have dissimilar values.
- A value near zero (and a non-significant $p$-value) indicates a random spatial pattern, with no evidence of spatial autocorrelation.

In the results above, several variables — diabetes prevalence, obesity, percent aged 65+, food environment index, PCP count, uninsured count, and SPR — typically show a positive and statistically significant Moran's I. Counties with high values tend to sit next to other high-value counties (and low next to low). Large $z$-scores confirm that this clustering is unlikely to be chance. This is the quantitative version of Tobler's First Law applied to county health data.

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
# Moran scatterplot: standardised diabetes vs its spatial lag
z_diab  <- as.numeric(scale(gdf$diabetes_prev))
Wz_diab <- lag.listw(lw_queen, z_diab, zero.policy = TRUE)
quadrant <- case_when(
  z_diab > 0 & Wz_diab > 0 ~ "High-High",
  z_diab < 0 & Wz_diab < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
  z_diab > 0 & Wz_diab < 0 ~ "High-Low",
  TRUE                     ~ "Low-High"
)
quad_colors <- c(
  "High-High" = "#D65F5F", "Low-Low" = "#4878CF",
  "High-Low"  = "#AEC6CF",  "Low-High" = "#F4A582"
)

p_scatter <- ggplot(tibble(z = z_diab, Wz = Wz_diab, q = quadrant),
                    aes(z, Wz, colour = q)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 0.9, stroke = 0) +
  geom_smooth(aes(z, Wz), method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black",
              linewidth = 0.9, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = quad_colors) +
  labs(
    x = "Standardised diabetes prevalence (z)",
    y = "Spatial lag (W*z)",
    colour = NULL,
    title = sprintf("Moran Scatterplot: Diabetes (%%)\n(I=%.3f, p=%.4g)", I_diab, p_diab)
  )

I_perm <- as.numeric(mc_diab$res[-length(mc_diab$res)])
p_perm <- ggplot(tibble(I = I_perm), aes(I)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#AEC6CF", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = I_diab, colour = "#D65F5F", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = e_diab, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Moran's I (permuted)", y = "Count",
    title = sprintf("Permutation distribution (B=199)\nMC p=%.4g", mc_diab$p.value)
  )

p_moran <- p_scatter | p_perm
print(p_moran)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "morans_i_diabetes.png"), p_moran,
       width = 14, height = 5, dpi = 150)
```

The slope of the Moran scatterplot equals (approximately) Moran's I: counties in the high-high and low-low quadrants pull $I$ up; high-low and low-high outliers pull it down.

## 4. Local Moran's I (LISA)

Local Moran's I (LISA) helps us find out *where* on the map we have clusters of high or low values — for example, groups of counties with similarly high diabetes prevalence (hot spots) or low rates (cold spots).

In simplest terms:

- For each county, LISA compares its value (diabetes prevalence) to its neighbours.
- It tells us if a county is surrounded by similar values ("cluster") or very different ones ("outlier").
- We can map these results to *see* local hot/cold spots.

The math, made simple. For each county $i$:

$$
I_i = \dfrac{(x_i - \bar{x})}{s^2} \sum_j w_{ij}(x_j - \bar{x})
$$

- $x_i$ = value at county $i$
- $\bar{x}$ = average value across all counties
- $w_{ij}$ = weight between county $i$ and neighbour $j$ (1 if neighbour, 0 if not, then row-standardised)
- $s^2$ = variance of all values

Interpretation:

- **High-High (HH)**: County and neighbours have high values (hot spot)
- **Low-Low (LL)**: County and neighbours have low values (cold spot)
- **High-Low (HL)**: High-value county among low-value neighbours (outlier)
- **Low-High (LH)**: Low-value county among high-value neighbours (outlier)
- **NS**: Not significant (no clear cluster/outlier)

In practical terms, LISA tells us not just *if* spatial clustering exists (like Moran's I), but *where* those clusters or outliers are on the map.

```{r}
lisa <- localmoran(gdf$diabetes_prev, lw_queen, zero.policy = TRUE)
gdf$lisa_i <- lisa[, "Ii"]
# Column name is stable across recent spdep versions
pcol <- grep("^Pr\\(", colnames(lisa), value = TRUE)[1]
gdf$lisa_p <- lisa[, pcol]

z_std <- as.numeric(scale(gdf$diabetes_prev))
z_lag <- lag.listw(lw_queen, z_std, zero.policy = TRUE)
quadrant_loc <- case_when(
  z_std > 0 & z_lag > 0 ~ "HH",
  z_std < 0 & z_lag < 0 ~ "LL",
  z_std > 0 & z_lag < 0 ~ "HL",
  TRUE                  ~ "LH"
)
gdf$lisa_cluster <- factor(
  ifelse(gdf$lisa_p < 0.05, quadrant_loc, "NS"),
  levels = c("HH", "LL", "HL", "LH", "NS")
)

cluster_colors <- c(
  HH = "#D65F5F", LL = "#4878CF", HL = "#F4A582", LH = "#92C5DE", NS = "#E0E0E0"
)

p_lisa <- ggplot(gdf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = lisa_cluster), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "LISA cluster map: adult diabetes (%)",
    subtitle = "HH = hot spots, LL = cold spots, HL/LH = outliers",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_map()

sig_lab <- factor(ifelse(gdf$lisa_p < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "NS"),
                  levels = c("p < 0.05", "NS"))
p_sig <- ggplot(gdf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = sig_lab), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = "#D65F5F", NS = "#E0E0E0"), drop = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = sprintf(
      "LISA significance map (p<0.05)\n%d significant counties (%.1f%%)",
      sum(gdf$lisa_p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean(gdf$lisa_p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
    ),
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_map()

p_lisa_both <- p_lisa | p_sig
print(p_lisa_both)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "lisa_cluster_map_diabetes.png"), p_lisa_both,
       width = 16, height = 6, dpi = 150)

cat("LISA cluster summary (diabetes):\n")
print(
  gdf %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    count(lisa_cluster, .drop = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)
)
```

The Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) cluster map reveals spatial patterns in county-level diabetes prevalence:

- **HH (High-High):** "Hot spot" counties with high diabetes rates surrounded by high-rate neighbours. These are potential priority regions for intervention.
- **LL (Low-Low):** "Cold spot" counties with low rates next to other low-rate counties, indicating healthier spatial clusters.
- **HL (High-Low):** High-rate counties surrounded by low-rate neighbours (potential spatial outliers).
- **LH (Low-High):** Low-rate counties surrounded by high-rate neighbours (also spatial outliers).
- **NS (Not Significant):** Counties where local Moran's I was not statistically significant ($p \ge 0.05$), indicating no strong local clustering.

The left plot shows cluster type; the right plot highlights which counties were significant at $p < 0.05$. Because 3,108 tests are run at once, treat unadjusted local $p$-values as exploratory — they are not Bonferroni-corrected.

## 5. Bivariate Local Moran's I

The **Bivariate Local Moran's I** asks whether the value of one variable at a location (diabetes in county $i$) is related to the values of a *different* variable in neighbouring locations (obesity in nearby counties).

**What does the bivariate statistic measure?**
- Are *high* diabetes rates in county $A$ surrounded by *high* obesity rates in neighbouring counties?
- Or are *low* diabetes rates surrounded by *low* obesity nearby?
- Or is there a mismatch between the two variables?

### Steps:

1. **Choose two variables:**
   - **$x$**: Value at the target location (diabetes prevalence in county $i$)
   - **$y$**: Value in each neighbouring location (obesity in surrounding counties)

2. **Standardise both variables:**
   - Subtract each variable's mean and divide by its standard deviation.
   - This gives both variables a *mean of 0* and *standard deviation of 1*.
   - $$
     z_{x,i} = \frac{x_i - \overline{x}}{s_x}
     $$
   - $$
     z_{y,j} = \frac{y_j - \overline{y}}{s_y}
     $$

3. **For each county $i$, calculate the bivariate Local Moran's I:**
   - $$
     I_i = z_{x,i} \times \left( \sum_j w_{ij} \cdot z_{y,j} \right)
     $$
   - Where $w_{ij}$ = spatial weight between county $i$ and neighbour $j$.
   - *Translation:* "How much is diabetes in county $i$ related to the (weighted) average obesity in its neighbours?"

4. **What does the value mean?**
   - **Large positive $I_i$**:
     - County $i$ has high diabetes, surrounded by neighbours with high obesity (*High-High cluster*), or
     - County $i$ has low diabetes, surrounded by low-obesity neighbours (*Low-Low cluster*).
   - **Large negative $I_i$**:
     - County $i$ is an *outlier*: for example, low diabetes in county $i$, but high obesity in neighbours (or vice versa).

5. **Easy analogy:**
   - Think of checking whether a high-diabetes county sits in a high-obesity neighbourhood — or whether it stands out as an exception among its neighbours.

> Bivariate Local Moran's I shows whether *the value of one variable* at a location (diabetes) is spatially associated with *the value of a different variable* nearby (obesity). It also reveals *where* these connections or mismatches occur on your map.

`spdep::localmoran_bv()` requires every county to have at least one neighbour, but two CONUS island counties have none under queen contiguity. We therefore compute $I_i = z_{x,i} \cdot (W z_y)$ with `lag.listw(..., zero.policy = TRUE)` and a local permutation of $z_y$ (`nsim = 199`). Island counties get lag 0.

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
zx  <- as.numeric(scale(gdf$diabetes_prev))
zy  <- as.numeric(scale(gdf$pct_obesity))
Wzy <- lag.listw(lw_queen, zy, zero.policy = TRUE)
Ii  <- zx * Wzy

set.seed(42)
nsim_bv <- 199
count_ext <- integer(length(Ii))
abs_Ii <- abs(Ii)
for (b in seq_len(nsim_bv)) {
  Wzy_p <- lag.listw(lw_queen, sample(zy), zero.policy = TRUE)
  count_ext <- count_ext + as.integer(abs(zx * Wzy_p) >= abs_Ii)
}
bv_p <- (count_ext + 1) / (nsim_bv + 1)

bv_quad <- case_when(
  zx > 0 & Wzy > 0 ~ "HH",
  zx < 0 & Wzy < 0 ~ "LL",
  zx > 0 & Wzy < 0 ~ "HL",
  TRUE             ~ "LH"
)
gdf$bivar_cluster <- factor(
  ifelse(!is.na(bv_p) & bv_p < 0.05, bv_quad, "NS"),
  levels = c("HH", "LL", "HL", "LH", "NS")
)

bv_colors <- c(
  HH = "#d73027", LL = "#4575b4", HL = "#fdae61", LH = "#abd9e9", NS = "#ffffbf"
)

p_bv <- ggplot(gdf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = bivar_cluster), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = bv_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Bivariate LISA: diabetes prevalence × obesity (neighbours)",
    subtitle = "I_i = z_diabetes,i × lag(z_obesity); permutation p from 199 draws",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_map()

print(p_bv)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "bivariate_lisa_diabetes_obesity.png"), p_bv,
       width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 150)

cat("Bivariate LISA cluster counts:\n")
print(
  gdf %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    count(bivar_cluster, .drop = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)
)
```

The bivariate Local Moran's I map colours each county by cluster type:

- **HH (High-High):** Counties with high diabetes surrounded by neighbours with high obesity — spatial "hot spots" for both variables.
- **LL (Low-Low):** Counties with low diabetes surrounded by low-obesity neighbours — "cold spots."
- **HL (High-Low):** High diabetes but neighbours with low obesity — spatial outliers.
- **LH (Low-High):** Low diabetes but neighbours with high obesity — the reverse outlier.
- **NS (Not Significant):** No significant spatial association at $p < 0.05$.

These clusters highlight places where diabetes and obesity reinforce each other geographically, and places that mismatch — useful for targeting interventions or investigating unusual regions.

## 6. Getis-Ord G* Hot Spot Analysis

The **Getis-Ord G\*** statistic finds "hot spots" (areas surrounded by other high-value areas) and "cold spots" (areas surrounded by other low-value areas).

### How does it work?

Imagine you want to know if a county with high diabetes is part of a hot spot (a cluster of high rates) or just a single high county in a sea of lower neighbours.

**Step-by-step:**

1. **Pick your variable:** diabetes prevalence in each county.

2. **For each county ($i$):**
   - Add up the rates in its "neighbourhood": itself **plus** all its neighbours.
   - (This is different from Moran's I, which skips itself!)

3. **Compare this local sum to the overall average:**
   - If the total for that area is **much higher than average**, it's a **hot spot**.
   - If it's **much lower**, it's a **cold spot**.

4. **The actual G\* statistic:**
   - It tells you (in standard-deviation units) how far above or below average this area's sum is compared to chance.
   - Big positive G\* = hot spot (lots of high values together).
   - Big negative G\* = cold spot (lots of low values together).

**Key idea:** G\* finds places where clusters of high or low values occur more often than you'd expect just by chance.

**Example:** "If my county plus my neighbours have much higher diabetes *together* than most, I show up as a hot spot."

**Getis-Ord G\* vs LISA (Local Moran's I):**

- **LISA:** Looks for spots where a place is "like its neighbours" (clusters) *and* places that are "unlike their neighbours" (outliers). The neighbourhood **excludes** the county itself.
- **Getis-Ord G\*:** Pinpoints hot spots or cold spots — but not outliers. The neighbourhood **includes** the county itself (`include.self()`).
- **LISA asks:** "Is my county's value surprisingly high/low *compared to* my neighbours? Am I part of a cluster, or an outlier?"
- **G\* asks:** "Do my county and its neighbours *together* have a sum much bigger/smaller than average?" Outliers (a high surrounded by lows) are not flagged.

Use LISA when you want clusters *and* outliers; use G\* when you want a simple hot/cold targeting map.

```{r}
# G* includes self; binary (non-standardised) weights
nb_gstar <- include.self(nb_queen)
lw_gstar <- nb2listw(nb_gstar, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
g_star <- localG(gdf$diabetes_prev, lw_gstar, zero.policy = TRUE)

gdf$g_star   <- as.numeric(g_star)
gdf$g_star_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(gdf$g_star))

gdf$hotspot_class <- factor(
  case_when(
    gdf$g_star >  2.58 ~ "Hot spot 99%",
    gdf$g_star >  1.96 ~ "Hot spot 95%",
    gdf$g_star < -2.58 ~ "Cold spot 99%",
    gdf$g_star < -1.96 ~ "Cold spot 95%",
    TRUE               ~ "Not significant"
  ),
  levels = c("Hot spot 99%", "Hot spot 95%", "Cold spot 95%",
             "Cold spot 99%", "Not significant")
)
hs_colors <- c(
  "Hot spot 99%"     = "#D73027",
  "Hot spot 95%"     = "#FC8D59",
  "Cold spot 95%"    = "#91BFDB",
  "Cold spot 99%"    = "#4575B4",
  "Not significant"  = "#E0E0E0"
)

p_hs <- ggplot(gdf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = hotspot_class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = hs_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Getis-Ord G* hot spot analysis: adult diabetes prevalence",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_map()

print(p_hs)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "getis_ord_gstar_diabetes.png"), p_hs,
       width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 150)

cat("G* class counts:\n")
print(
  gdf %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    count(hotspot_class, .drop = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)
)
```

1. Global Moran's I $= 0.42$ ($p < 0.001$). Does this statistic inform us about the *location* of spatial clusters? Explain.
2. A LISA map identifies an HL (High-Low) outlier — a county with high diabetes surrounded by counties with low diabetes. List three plausible reasons for such a spatial outlier:
   - (a) __
   - (b) __
   - (c) __
3. If you switched from queen contiguity weights to k-nearest neighbour ($k = 8$) spatial weights, how would you expect the calculated Moran's I to change? Why?
4. When interpreting LISA $p$-values, why is it important to be cautious given that 3,108 local tests are conducted simultaneously?
5. Calculate Moran's I for the *residuals* from an OLS regression of diabetes on obesity, SPR, and uninsured count. What does the result tell you about spatial dependence after adjustment?

```{r}
# Exercise 5 — Moran's I on OLS residuals vs raw diabetes
ols <- lm(diabetes_prev ~ pct_obesity + smr + n_uninsured, data = gdf)
mt_raw  <- moran.test(gdf$diabetes_prev, lw_queen,
                      zero.policy = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided")
mt_ols  <- moran.test(residuals(ols), lw_queen,
                      zero.policy = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided")

cat(sprintf("OLS R-squared: %.4f\n", summary(ols)$r.squared))
cat(sprintf(
  "Moran's I on diabetes prevalence : %.4f (p=%.4g)\n",
  unname(mt_raw$estimate["Moran I statistic"]), mt_raw$p.value
))
cat(sprintf(
  "Moran's I on OLS residuals       : %.4f (p=%.4g)\n",
  unname(mt_ols$estimate["Moran I statistic"]), mt_ols$p.value
))
cat("Note: SPR (smr) is diabetes / national mean, so it is a rescaling of the outcome;\n")
cat("residual Moran's I will drop sharply. Compare with a non-circular specification\n")
cat("in NB-03 (diabetes ~ obesity + % aged 65+ + uninsured).\n")

if (mt_ols$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("Significant residual spatial autocorrelation -> OLS inference is suspect.\n")
  cat("Need spatial regression models (spatial lag or spatial error) — see NB-03.\n")
} else {
  cat("Residual spatial autocorrelation is not significant after this adjustment.\n")
}
```
